claim: Over half of the human population is colonized by Helicobacter pylori.
source: Over half of the human population is colonized by the motile gram-negative bacteria, Helicobacter pylori.
evidence: This is a general statement about H. pylori prevalence in humans, presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: H. pylori infections have been implicated in peptic ulcers and non-cardia gastric cancer.
source: H. pylori infections have been implicated in peptic ulcers as well as non-cardia gastric cancer (Peek and Blaser, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Peek and Blaser, 2002.

claim: H. pylori infections are promoted by the bacterium's ability to swim with flagella.
source: Infections are promoted by the ability of the bacterium to swim with the aid of helical appendages called flagella (Aihara et al., 2014; Ottemann and Lowenthal, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aihara et al., 2014 and Ottemann and Lowenthal, 2002.

claim: The flagellar filaments in H. pylori are rotated by transmembrane flagellar motors that repeatedly switch their direction of rotation.
source: The flagellar filaments are rotated by transmembrane flagellar motors that repeatedly switch their direction of rotation.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of flagellar rotation, presented as established knowledge.

claim: H. pylori flagellar filaments are located unipolarly and are left-handed.
source: Owing to the unipolar location of the left-handed flagellar filaments (Constantino et al., 2016), counterclockwise (CCW) rotation of the motors causes the cell to run with the flagella lagging behind the body – a mode of motility termed as the pusher mode.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Constantino et al., 2016.

claim: Counterclockwise rotation of H. pylori motors causes the cell to run in the pusher mode with flagella lagging behind the body.
source: Owing to the unipolar location of the left-handed flagellar filaments (Constantino et al., 2016), counterclockwise (CCW) rotation of the motors causes the cell to run with the flagella lagging behind the body – a mode of motility termed as the pusher mode.
evidence: This claim combines citation-based information about filament structure with logical inference about the resulting swimming mode.

claim: The cell reverses with the body lagging the flagella when the motors switch to clockwise rotation.
source: The cell reverses with the body lagging the flagella when the motors switch the direction of rotation to clockwise (CW). This mode of motility is termed as the puller mode (Lauga and Powers, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lauga and Powers, 2009.

claim: Modulation of reversals between pusher and puller modes enables H. pylori to undergo chemotaxis.
source: Modulation of the reversals between the two modes enables the cell to undergo chemotaxis — migration toward favorable chemical habitats (Lertsethtakarn et al., 2011; Howitt et al., 2011; Johnson and Ottemann, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lertsethtakarn et al., 2011; Howitt et al., 2011; and Johnson and Ottemann, 2018.

claim: The core chemotaxis network in H. pylori is similar to that in E. coli.
source: The core chemotaxis network is similar to that in E. coli (Lertsethtakarn et al., 2011; Abedrabbo et al., 2017; Lertsethtakarn et al., 2015; Lowenthal et al., 2009b; Pittman et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Several components that form the flagellar motor in H. pylori are similar to those in E. coli.
source: Several components that form the flagellar motor are also similar to those in E. coli (Lertsethtakarn et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lertsethtakarn et al., 2011.

claim: How the chemotaxis network modulates flagellar functions in H. pylori remains unknown.
source: How the chemotaxis network modulates flagellar functions in H. pylori remains unknown (Lertsethtakarn et al., 2011; Lertsethtakarn et al., 2015; Jiménez-Pearson et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations indicating a knowledge gap.

claim: In the canonical chemotaxis network, chemoreceptors sense extracellular ligands and modulate the activity of the chemotaxis kinase.
source: In the canonical chemotaxis network, chemoreceptors sense extracellular ligands and modulate the activity of the chemotaxis kinase, which in turn modulates CheY-P levels.
evidence: This is a statement about the canonical chemotaxis network, presented as established knowledge.

claim: Increased CheY-P binding to the motor promotes CW rotation in an otherwise CCW rotating motor in the canonical chemotaxis network.
source: Increased CheY-P binding to the motor promotes CW rotation in an otherwise CCW rotating motor (Sourjik and Wingreen, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sourjik and Wingreen, 2012.

claim: CWbias is defined as the fraction of time that the motor rotates CW.
source: The output of the flagellar switch is quantified by the fraction of the time that the motor rotates CW, termed CWbias (Block et al., 1983; Yuan et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Block et al., 1983; Yuan et al., 2012; and Yang et al., 2020.

claim: A decrease in CheY-P levels causes a corresponding decrease in CWbias.
source: A decrease (increase) in CheY-P levels causes corresponding decrease (increase) in CWbias (Cluzel et al., 2000; Scharf et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cluzel et al., 2000 and Scharf et al., 1998.

claim: An increase in CheY-P levels causes a corresponding increase in CWbias.
source: A decrease (increase) in CheY-P levels causes corresponding decrease (increase) in CWbias (Cluzel et al., 2000; Scharf et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cluzel et al., 2000 and Scharf et al., 1998.

claim: Dynamic variations in CWbias sensitively report changes in kinase activity due to external stimuli and internal noise in the network.
source: Thus, dynamic variations in the CWbias sensitively report changes in the kinase activity due to external stimuli as well as due to the internal noise in the network (Cluzel et al., 2000; Korobkova et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cluzel et al., 2000 and Korobkova et al., 2004.

claim: The frequency at which motors switch direction does not accurately represent changes in chemotaxis output.
source: In contrast, the frequency at which motors switch their direction does not accurately represent changes in the chemotaxis output as the frequency decreases when CheY-P levels increase as well as when CheY-P levels decrease (Cluzel et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cluzel et al., 2000.

claim: Prior work on H. pylori has focused on the effects of extracellular ligands on the frequency of cell reversals rather than motor bias.
source: Prior work has focused on the effects of extracellular ligands on the frequency of cell reversals (Collins et al., 2016; Machuca et al., 2017; Goers Sweeney et al., 2012; Rader et al., 2011; Sanders et al., 2013; Schweinitzer et al., 2008) rather than the motor bias.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: It is unknown whether the chemotaxis network in H. pylori modulates the rotational bias.
source: It is unknown whether the chemotaxis network in H. pylori modulates the rotational bias.
evidence: This is a statement about a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Discriminating between the swimming modes of single H. pylori cells is difficult due to technical challenges in visualizing flagellar filaments in swimmers.
source: However, discriminating between the swimming modes of single H. pylori cells is difficult owing to the technical challenges in visualizing flagellar filaments in swimmers (Constantino et al., 2016; Lowenthal et al., 2009a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Constantino et al., 2016 and Lowenthal et al., 2009a.

claim: A popular method to quantify CWbias is by monitoring the rotation of tethered cells.
source: A popular method to quantify the CWbias is by monitoring the rotation of tethered cells, where a single flagellar filament is attached to a glass surface while the cell freely rotates (Block et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Block et al., 1983.

claim: The bias can be determined by sticking the cell to the surface and monitoring the rotation of a probe bead attached to a single flagellar filament.
source: Alternatively, the bias is determined by sticking the cell to the surface and monitoring the rotation of a probe bead attached to a single flagellar filament (Ford et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ford et al., 2017 and Yuan et al., 2010.

claim: In H. pylori, the flagella are distributed in close proximity to one another at a single pole.
source: In H. pylori, however, the flagella are distributed in close proximity to one another at a single pole (Qin et al., 2017), increasing the likelihood of tethering more than one filament.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Qin et al., 2017.

claim: Tethering of multiple flagella on the same H. pylori cell eliminates rotational degrees of freedom, inhibiting motor function.
source: Tethering of multiple flagella on the same cell eliminates rotational degrees of freedom, inhibiting motor function.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of tethering multiple flagella.

claim: Crucial features of the signaling network in H. pylori remain unknown due to limited measurements of CWbias.
source: Because of the limited measurements of the CWbias, crucial features of the signaling network, such as the dynamic range of signal detection, adaptation mechanisms, and the roles of key chemotaxis-related proteins, remain unknown in H. pylori.
evidence: This is a statement about knowledge gaps in the field.

claim: H. pylori swim faster whenever their flagella rotate counterclockwise.
source: Here, we determined that H. pylori swim faster (slower) whenever their flagella rotate counterclockwise (clockwise) by analyzing their hydrodynamic interactions with bounding surfaces.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the study analyzing hydrodynamic interactions.

claim: H. pylori swim slower whenever their flagella rotate clockwise.
source: Here, we determined that H. pylori swim faster (slower) whenever their flagella rotate counterclockwise (clockwise) by analyzing their hydrodynamic interactions with bounding surfaces.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the study analyzing hydrodynamic interactions.

claim: Upon exposure to a chemoattractant, the bias decreased and H. pylori cells tended to swim exclusively in the faster mode.
source: Upon exposure to a chemo-attractant, the bias decreased and the cells tended to swim exclusively in the faster mode.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the study.

claim: In the absence of CheY, the rotational bias in H. pylori was zero.
source: In the absence of a key chemotaxis protein, CheY, the bias was zero.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the study using a CheY deletion mutant.

claim: The relationship between the reversal frequency and the rotational bias in H. pylori was unimodal.
source: The relationship between the reversal frequency and the rotational bias was unimodal.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the study.

claim: H. pylori's chemotaxis network modulates the probability of clockwise rotation in otherwise counterclockwise-rotating flagella, similar to the canonical network.
source: Thus, H. pylori's chemotaxis network appears to modulate the probability of clockwise rotation in otherwise counterclockwise-rotating flagella, similar to the canonical network.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The flick of the flagellum that causes turn angles to be distributed around 90° in Vibrio alginolyticus is unlikely to occur in H. pylori.
source: The flick of the flagellum that causes turn angles to be distributed ~90° in another run-reversing species Vibrio alginolyticus (Stocker, 2011), is unlikely to occur in H. pylori.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the turn angle data and comparison with V. alginolyticus, supported by a citation.

claim: Mean speeds in alternate bins were anti-correlated in H. pylori: each reversal either decreased or increased the speed.
source: Mean speeds in alternate bins were anti-correlated: each reversal either decreased or increased the speed.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the study.

claim: The speeds in the two swimming modes of H. pylori were unequal.
source: This suggested that the speeds in the two modes were unequal.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the anti-correlation of speeds in alternate bins.

claim: The speed in the fast mode was approximately 1.5 times the speed in the slow mode in H. pylori.
source: The speed in the fast mode was ~1.5 times the speed in the slow mode.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A recent study suggested that H. pylori cells swim faster in the pusher mode, but sample sizes were severely limited by difficulties in visualizing flagella on swimmers.
source: A recent study attempted to visualize the flagella in H. pylori with high-magnification microscopy, and suggested that the cells swim faster in the pusher mode. However, the sample sizes were severely limited by the difficulties in visualizing flagella on the swimmers (Constantino et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Constantino et al., 2016.

claim: Cells that swim very close to an underlying solid boundary exhibit circular trajectories owing to increased viscous drag on the bottom of the cell and flagellar filaments.
source: Cells that swim very close to an underlying solid boundary exhibit circular trajectories owing to the increased viscous drag on the bottom of the cell and the flagellar filaments.
evidence: This is a statement about hydrodynamic interactions, presented as established knowledge.

claim: CCW rotation of the left-handed helical filament causes the pusher to experience a lateral force that promotes CW circular tracks.
source: CCW rotation of the left-handed helical filament causes the pusher to experience a lateral force that promotes CW circular tracks (Figure 2A, DiLuzio et al., 2005; Lauga et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to DiLuzio et al., 2005 and Lauga et al., 2006, and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: For each H. pylori cell analyzed, the CW trajectories were always faster relative to the CCW trajectories.
source: For each cell, the CW trajectories were always faster relative to the CCW trajectories, indicating that the pusher mode was the faster mode (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The pusher mode is the faster mode in H. pylori.
source: For each cell, the CW trajectories were always faster relative to the CCW trajectories, indicating that the pusher mode was the faster mode (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing CW trajectories are faster.

claim: The mean ratio of the speeds of the CW trajectories to that of the respective CCW trajectories was approximately 1.6 ± 0.5 over 116 cells.
source: This was confirmed over n = 116 cells; the mean ratio of the speeds of the CW trajectories to that of the respective CCW trajectories was ~1.6 ± 0.5 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The CWbias in H. pylori was similar to that observed in E. coli.
source: The bias was similar to that observed in E. coli (Block et al., 1983; Segall et al., 1986; Ford et al., 2018; Sagawa et al., 2014; Block et al., 1982; Stock et al., 1985), suggesting that the basal chemotactic output in the two species is similar.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of experimental data with cited literature.

claim: The basal chemotactic output in H. pylori and E. coli is similar.
source: The bias was similar to that observed in E. coli (Block et al., 1983; Segall et al., 1986; Ford et al., 2018; Sagawa et al., 2014; Block et al., 1982; Stock et al., 1985), suggesting that the basal chemotactic output in the two species is similar.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity in CWbias between the two species.

claim: Most H. pylori cells tended to rotate their motors CCW for a higher fraction of time.
source: As evident, most cells tended to rotate their motors CCW for a higher fraction of time.
evidence: This claim is based on the CWbias distribution data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ΔcheY mutant H. pylori cells swam in CW-only trajectories, which indicate CCW flagellar rotation.
source: Next, we imaged swimmers belonging to a cheY-deleted strain and observed that the trajectories of cells near a surface were exclusively CW circles.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the ΔcheY mutant shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The default direction of flagellar rotation in H. pylori is CCW, similar to E. coli.
source: This suggested that the default direction of flagellar rotation is CCW, similar to E. coli (Ford et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ΔcheY mutant data and supported by citations to E. coli studies.

claim: CheY-P binding likely promotes CW rotation in an otherwise CCW rotating motor in H. pylori.
source: Considering that the bias is zero in the absence and ~0.35 in the presence of CheY, CheY-P binding likely promotes CW rotation in an otherwise CCW rotating motor in H. pylori.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of CWbias in wild-type and ΔcheY mutant cells.

claim: Urea is a potent chemoattractant for H. pylori.
source: We stimulated cells by adding them to a bath of urea (20 mM in motility buffer-MB, see Materials and methods), which is a potent chemoattractant for H. pylori (Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Huang et al., 2015.

claim: Following exposure to urea, the majority of H. pylori cells swam exclusively in the pusher mode with post-stimulus CWbias approximately 0.
source: Following exposure to the attractant, the majority of the cells swam exclusively in the pusher mode – their post-stimulus CWbias was ~0 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The reversal frequency decreased in H. pylori in response to the chemoattractant urea.
source: The reversal frequency also decreased in response to the chemo-attractant (Figure 3D), which is in agreement with previous reports (Machuca et al., 2017; Perkins et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3D and supported by citations.

claim: A reduction in kinase activity upon sensing of chemoattractants inhibits the rotational bias of flagellar motors in H. pylori, similar to E. coli.
source: These observations are consistent with the notion that a reduction in the kinase activity upon the sensing of chemo-attractants inhibits the rotational bias of flagellar motors, similar to how the chemotaxis network modulates the response of E. coli to attractants (Block et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and supported by a citation to E. coli studies.

claim: The mean pusher and puller speeds in H. pylori trended upwards with temperature.
source: The mean pusher and puller speeds trended upwards with the temperature (Figure 4A, left panel), presumably through modulation of proton translocation kinetics that power the motor (Yuan and Berg, 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A and supported by a citation.

claim: The ratio of the speeds in the pusher and puller modes appeared to be independent of temperature in H. pylori.
source: The ratio of the speeds in the two modes appeared to be independent of the temperature (Figure 4A, right panel).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The responses of H. pylori swimming speeds to temperature are consistent with experiments in E. coli that show a strong influence of temperatures on the rotational speeds of the flagellar motor.
source: These responses are consistent with experiments in E. coli that show a strong influence of temperatures on the rotational speeds of the flagellar motor (Yuan and Berg, 2010; Turner et al., 1996; Turner et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with cited E. coli studies.

claim: The frequency of reversals in H. pylori increased steadily with temperature up to 37°C.
source: The frequency of reversals increased steadily with temperature up to 37°C, whereas the steady-state CWbias varied weakly with temperature (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The steady-state CWbias in H. pylori varied weakly with temperature.
source: The frequency of reversals increased steadily with temperature up to 37°C, whereas the steady-state CWbias varied weakly with temperature (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At room temperatures, the CWbias in H. pylori was the lowest, indicating that cells mostly prefer to swim in the pusher mode.
source: At room temperatures, the CWbias was the lowest, indicating that the cells mostly prefer to swim in the pusher mode.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data and inference about swimming mode preference.

claim: The reversal frequency in H. pylori was maximum at approximately 0.4 CWbias and decreased on either side.
source: The reversal frequency was maximum at ~0.4﻿ CWbias and decreased on either side (Figure 4C); also see Appendix 3—figure 1.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The reversal frequency in H. pylori has a unimodal dependence on CheY-P levels.
source: As our results suggest that CheY-P binding increases the CWbias (Figure 3B,C), this also means that the reversal frequency has a similar unimodal dependence on CheY-P levels.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the unimodal relationship between reversal frequency and CWbias, combined with the relationship between CheY-P and CWbias.

claim: Changes in the reversal frequency in H. pylori cannot provide accurate information about the effect of stimulants on the kinase activity.
source: Hence, we propose that changes in the reversal frequency in H. pylori cannot provide accurate information about the effect of stimulants on the kinase activity (i.e. whether a stimulant increases or decreases the activity).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the unimodal relationship between reversal frequency and CWbias/CheY-P levels.

claim: The rotational bias is likely a better measure of the kinase activity in H. pylori than reversal frequency, similar to E. coli.
source: On the other hand, the rotational bias is likely a better measure of the kinase activity, similar to that in E. coli.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the analysis of reversal frequency and CWbias relationships.

claim: In E. coli, flagellar switching has been well described by a two-state model where CheY-P binding stabilizes the CW conformation.
source: In E. coli, flagellar switching has been well described by a two-state model, where the binding of phosphorylated CheY (CheY-P) to the flagellar switch stabilizes the CW conformation (Turner et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Turner et al., 1999.

claim: In the absence of CheY-P, the probability of observing CW rotation in an otherwise CCW-rotating motor decreases with increasing temperatures in E. coli.
source: In the absence of CheY-P, the probability of observing CW rotation in an otherwise CCW-rotating motor decreases with increasing temperatures (Turner et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Turner et al., 1996.

claim: The chemotaxis network in E. coli adapts such that the steady-state levels of CheY-P are independent of temperatures.
source: The chemotaxis network itself adapts such that the steady-state levels of CheY-P are independent of the temperatures (Paulick et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Paulick et al., 2017.

claim: Assuming CheY-P levels are independent of temperature in H. pylori, the relative insensitivity of the rotational bias suggested that the dissociation constant for CheY-P/switch interactions likely decreased with rising temperatures.
source: Assuming that CheY-P levels are also independent of the temperature in H. pylori, the relative insensitivity of the rotational bias in Figure 4B suggested that the dissociation constant for CheY-P/switch interactions likely decreased with rising temperatures.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and assumptions about CheY-P levels.

claim: Assuming CheY-P levels are approximately 3 μM, the dissociation constant for CheY-P/switch interactions in H. pylori is estimated to be approximately 9 μM at 37°C.
source: Assuming that the CheY-P levels are ~3 μM (Cluzel et al., 2000), we estimate the dissociation constant to be ~9 μM at 37°C.
evidence: This claim is based on calculations using experimental data and assumptions, with a citation for the CheY-P level assumption.

claim: Motility enhances the spread of bacteria, lending a significant advantage over immotile bacteria in exploring three-dimensional spaces.
source: Even without chemotaxis, motility enhances the spread of bacteria, lending a significant advantage over immotile bacteria in exploring three-dimensional spaces (Josenhans and Suerbaum, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Josenhans and Suerbaum, 2002.

claim: Bacterial motion becomes uncorrelated over long times and large length-scales in the absence of a signal.
source: Bacterial motion becomes uncorrelated over long times and large length-scales in the absence of a signal.
evidence: This is a statement about bacterial motion, presented as established knowledge.

claim: Several previous works have modeled the diffusion of motile bacteria by assuming that the reversal wait-times are exponentially distributed.
source: Several previous works have modeled the diffusion of motile bacteria by assuming that the reversal wait-times are exponentially distributed (Berg, 1993; Lovely and Dahlquist, 1975; Lauga, 2016; Theves et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In some bacterial species that exhibit runs and reversals, the wait-time is Gamma distributed.
source: In some bacterial species that exhibit runs and reversals, the wait-time is Gamma distributed (Theves et al., 2013; Morse et al., 2016; Xie et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Theves et al., 2013; Morse et al., 2016; and Xie et al., 2011.

claim: The assumption of exponentially distributed wait-times leads to inaccurate predictions in bacterial species with Gamma distributed wait-times.
source: The assumption of exponentially distributed wait-times leads to inaccurate predictions in such species (Theves et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Theves et al., 2013.

claim: The reversal wait-times in H. pylori were Gamma distributed.
source: Our cell-tracking analysis revealed that the reversal wait-times were Gamma distributed in H. pylori (Figure 5A, also see separate distributions for the two swimming modes in Appendix 3—figure 2).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The simulated diffuse spread was low when H. pylori cells covered similar distances in the forward and backward directions.
source: As shown in Figure 5D, the simulated diffuse spread was low when cells covered similar distances in the forward and backward directions, thereby minimizing net displacement.
evidence: This claim is based on simulation results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In H. pylori, the tendency to spend more time in the faster pusher mode (basal CWbias approximately 0.35) is advantageous for diffusive spread.
source: Thus, in H. pylori, the tendency to spend more time in the faster pusher mode (basal CWbias ~ 0.35, Figure 3A) is advantageous (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the simulation results and experimental data.

claim: A very low basal value of CWbias is disadvantageous from a chemotaxis perspective in H. pylori.
source: However, a very low basal value of the CWbias is disadvantageous from a chemotaxis perspective.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about chemotaxis requirements.

claim: H. pylori respond to attractants by reducing their CWbias.
source: H. pylori appear to respond to attractants by reducing their CWbias (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: H. pylori would lose their ability to respond to attractants if the pre-stimulus (basal) bias was close to its minimum value (=0).
source: They would lose their ability to respond to attractants if the pre-stimulus (basal) bias was close to its minimum value (=0).
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the requirements for chemotaxis response.

claim: The basal activity of the chemotaxis network is possibly optimized in asymmetrically run-reversing bacteria to promote higher diffusive spread while retaining the ability to respond to chemical stimuli.
source: It is possible, therefore, that the basal activity of the chemotaxis network is optimized in asymmetrically run-reversing bacteria to promote higher diffusive spread while retaining the ability to respond to chemical stimuli.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental and simulation data.

claim: Longer durations of runs and reversals helped H. pylori cells cover larger distances.
source: Finally, longer durations of runs and reversals helped cells cover larger distances.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between run duration and distance covered.

claim: The diffusion coefficient in H. pylori was inversely dependent on the run-reversal frequency.
source: Thus, the diffusion coefficient was inversely dependent on the run-reversal frequency (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions shown in Figure 5E.

claim: As the reversal frequencies reach a maximum at 37°C, it is possible that H. pylori cells at physiological temperatures spread slower in a niche over long times, providing more time for cells to adhere to surfaces.
source: As the reversal frequencies reach a maximum at 37°C (Figure 4B), it is possible that cells at physiological temperatures spread slower in a niche over long times, providing more time for cells to adhere to surfaces.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The flagellar motors in H. pylori rotate CCW by default.
source: Our experiments with a mutant lacking cheY showed that the flagellar motors in H. pylori rotate CCW by default (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the ΔcheY mutant shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At native CheY-P levels, motors in wild-type H. pylori cells spent about 35% of the time rotating CW.
source: At native CheY-P levels, motors in wild-type cells spent about 35% of the time rotating CW (Figure 3A) – thus, the probability of CW rotation increases with CheY.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The probability of CW rotation in H. pylori increases with CheY.
source: At native CheY-P levels, motors in wild-type cells spent about 35% of the time rotating CW (Figure 3A) – thus, the probability of CW rotation increases with CheY.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of CWbias in wild-type and ΔcheY mutant cells.

claim: Treatment of wild-type H. pylori cells with urea decreased the rotational bias (CWbias).
source: Our experiments further showed that treatment of wild-type cells with a potent attractant (urea) decreased the rotational bias (CWbias).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The chemotaxis network in H. pylori controls the levels of CheY-P to modulate the probability of CW rotation in an otherwise CCW rotating flagellar motor.
source: These results are consistent with a model in which the chemotaxis network controls the levels of CheY-P to modulate the probability of CW rotation in an otherwise CCW rotating flagellar motor.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results with the ΔcheY mutant and attractant response.

claim: The chemotaxis networks in E. coli and H. pylori modulate flagellar functions in a similar manner.
source: If so, then the chemotaxis networks in the two species, E. coli and H. pylori, modulate flagellar functions in a similar manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of chemotaxis mechanisms in the two species.

claim: Earlier works focused exclusively on the effect of chemoeffectors on steady-state reversal frequencies in H. pylori to characterize chemotaxis responses.
source: Earlier works focused exclusively on the effect of chemoeffectors on steady-state reversal frequencies in H. pylori to characterize chemotaxis responses (Collins et al., 2016; Machuca et al., 2017; Goers Sweeney et al., 2012; Rader et al., 2011; Sanders et al., 2013; Schweinitzer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Increases in reversal frequency might help a H. pylori cell linger in a niche because diffusion scales inversely with reversal frequency.
source: Because diffusion scales inversely with the reversal frequency (Figure 5E), increases in frequency might help a cell linger in a niche.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the model predictions about diffusion and reversal frequency.

claim: Mere variations of the steady-state reversal frequencies with local stimulant concentrations or temperatures does not enable chemotaxis.
source: However, mere variations of the steady-state reversal frequencies with the local stimulant concentrations (or temperatures) does not enable chemotaxis (Berg, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berg, 1993.

claim: The dependence of the reversal frequency on the rotational bias is unimodal in H. pylori, similar to E. coli.
source: By combining data collected over a range of temperatures, we showed that the dependence of the reversal frequency on the rotational bias is unimodal (Figure 4C). This means that the reversal frequency does not have a unique value with respect to the rotational bias (other than at maximal frequency), similar to that in E. coli (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C and comparison with E. coli data in Figure 6A.

claim: The reversal frequency does not have a unique value with respect to the rotational bias in H. pylori (other than at maximal frequency).
source: This means that the reversal frequency does not have a unique value with respect to the rotational bias (other than at maximal frequency), similar to that in E. coli (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the unimodal relationship between reversal frequency and CWbias.

claim: The reversal frequency value is unlikely to be unique with respect to the kinase activity in H. pylori.
source: Hence, the reversal frequency value is also unlikely to be unique with respect to the kinase activity (the corresponding relationship in E. coli is depicted in Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the unimodal relationship between reversal frequency and CWbias, and the relationship between CWbias and kinase activity.

claim: Changes in the reversal frequencies by themselves are unlikely to accurately report changes in the chemotaxis output in H. pylori.
source: Therefore, changes in the reversal frequencies by themselves are unlikely to accurately report changes in the chemotaxis output in H. pylori.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the unimodal relationship between reversal frequency and chemotaxis output.

claim: The rotational bias must be quantified to accurately determine the chemotaxis output in H. pylori.
source: Our results suggest that the rotational bias must be quantified to accurately determine the chemotaxis output in H. pylori.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the analysis of reversal frequency and CWbias relationships.

claim: To prevent the cell from tumbling during a reversal, all the flagellar motors in a single cell of H. pylori must switch synchronously from one direction to the other.
source: To prevent the cell from tumbling during a reversal, all the flagellar motors in a single cell of H. pylori must switch synchronously from one direction to the other.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for coordinated switching.

claim: Tumbles were rarely observed in H. pylori.
source: Indeed, tumbles were rarely observed.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: The most frequent turn angles in H. pylori were approximately 180°, which confirmed that cells retraced their paths following a reversal.
source: The most frequent turn angles were ~180°, which confirmed that the cells retraced their paths following a reversal – this would not have been the case if only a fraction of the motors switched to the opposite direction.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: One possibility for how multiple stochastic switchers are coupled in H. pylori is that the flagellar switch is ultrasensitive to small fluctuations in CheY-P levels, similar to E. coli.
source: How are such multiple stochastic switchers coupled in H. pylori? One possibility is that the flagellar switch in H. pylori is ultrasensitive to small fluctuations in CheY-P levels, similar to the switch in E. coli (Cluzel et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on comparison with E. coli and supported by a citation.

claim: The close proximity of the multiple motors at a single pole in H. pylori means that the local concentration of CheY-P in the vicinity of each flagellar switch is similar.
source: The close proximity of the multiple motors at a single pole in H. pylori also means that the local concentration of CheY-P in the vicinity of each flagellar switch is similar.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of motor proximity.

claim: Similar local CheY-P concentrations increase the probability of concerted switching in all the motors in H. pylori.
source: This increases the probability of concerted switching in all the motors.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of similar CheY-P concentrations.

claim: In V. alginolyticus, asymmetry in swimming speeds has been observed only near bounding surfaces but not in the bulk fluid.
source: In V. alginolyticus, asymmetry in swimming speeds has been observed only near bounding surfaces but not in the bulk fluid (Magariyama et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Magariyama et al., 2005.

claim: A limitation of the speed asymmetry method is that it is unsuitable for tracking chemotaxis response dynamics in species where asymmetry is lost when cells migrate away from surfaces.
source: A limitation of our method is that it is unsuitable for tracking chemotaxis response dynamics in such species, as the asymmetry is lost whenever the cells migrate away from surfaces.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of the method.

claim: In H. pylori, asymmetric speeds were observed in some cells even at a separation of approximately 200 μm from any bounding surfaces.
source: In H. pylori, although, we observed asymmetric speeds in some cells even at a separation of ~200 μm from any bounding surfaces (see Appendix 6), similar to Pseudomonas putida (Theves et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations and comparison with P. putida.

claim: The asymmetry in swimming speeds is unlikely to be a surface-effect in H. pylori.
source: Therefore, the asymmetry is unlikely to be a surface-effect in H. pylori.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of asymmetry far from surfaces.

claim: The asymmetry in swimming speeds could be due to differences in the flagellar shape and forms or the swimming gait in the pusher and puller modes.
source: The effect could be due to differences in the flagellar shape and forms (Kinosita et al., 2018) or the swimming gait in the pusher and puller modes (Lele et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on citations to relevant studies.

claim: It is more likely that the asymmetry in speeds in H. pylori arises due to differences in the CW and CCW flagellar rotational speeds.
source: It is more likely that the asymmetry in speeds arises due to the differences in the CW and CCW flagellar rotational speeds, as is the case with E. coli – which run and tumble – and Caulobacter cresecentus (Yuan et al., 2010; Lele et al., 2016) – which exhibit symmetric swimming speeds in the pusher and puller modes (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on comparison with other species and supported by citations.

claim: Differences in the speeds at which motors rotate CW and CCW depend on the external viscous loads.
source: Such differences in the speeds at which motors rotate CW and CCW depend on the external viscous loads (Yuan et al., 2010; Lele et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yuan et al., 2010 and Lele et al., 2016.

claim: It is possible that the asymmetry in H. pylori is load-dependent, vanishing for longer filament lengths in highly viscous microenvironments or for very short filaments.
source: It is possible therefore, that the asymmetry in H. pylori is also load-dependent; vanishing for longer filament lengths in highly viscous microenvironments or for very short filaments.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the load-dependence of motor speed differences.

claim: The asymmetry in swimming speeds is expected to depend sensitively on the expression of the flagellar genes, which is modulated by environmental conditions.
source: The asymmetry is further expected to depend sensitively on the expression of the flagellar genes, which is modulated by environmental conditions (Spohn and Scarlato, 1999).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference and supported by a citation.

claim: The asymmetry in swimming speeds was prominently observable with careful control of experimental conditions.
source: The asymmetry was prominently observable in our work with a careful control of experimental conditions (Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental approach described in the manuscript.

claim: The flagellar motors in H. pylori and E. coli share structural similarities and have several orthologous components.
source: The flagellar motors in H. pylori and E. coli share structural similarities and have several orthologous components.
evidence: This is a statement about structural similarities, presented as established knowledge.

claim: The core chemotaxis network in H. pylori and E. coli is similar with the exception of a few enzymes.
source: The core chemotaxis network in the two species is also similar with the exception of a few enzymes (Lertsethtakarn et al., 2011; Howitt et al., 2011; Lertsethtakarn et al., 2015; Jiménez-Pearson et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CheY, in its phosphorylated form, modulates flagellar functions in both H. pylori and E. coli by interacting with components of the flagellar switch.
source: CheY, in its phosphorylated form, modulates flagellar functions in both species by interacting with components of the flagellar switch (Lertsethtakarn et al., 2011; Lowenthal et al., 2009a; Qin et al., 2017; Lam et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The regulatory function of CheY-P is similar in H. pylori and E. coli: CheY-P binding to the motor increases the probability of CW rotation.
source: Our results suggest that the regulatory function of CheY-P is also similar in the two species, that is, CheY-P binding to the motor increases the probability of CW rotation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: Because H. pylori can retrace their paths upon a reversal unlike E. coli, modulation of the rotational bias is bound to undermine chemotaxis when the cell enters the puller mode.
source: Because H. pylori can retrace their paths upon a reversal unlike E. coli, modulation of the rotational bias is bound to undermine chemotaxis when the cell enters the puller mode.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of path retracing for chemotaxis.

claim: H. pylori would likely need a mechanism to rectify its movements with respect to the source or some type of feedback between the motors and the receptors to successfully migrate in response to chemical gradients.
source: Then, the cell would likely need a mechanism to rectify its movements with respect to the source or some type of feedback between the motors and the receptors to successfully migrate in response to chemical gradients.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference about chemotaxis requirements.

claim: The approach described in this work is extensible to any run-reversing species that exhibit asymmetric swimming speeds.
source: Our approach is extensible to any run-reversing species that exhibit asymmetric swimming speeds, paving the way to study signaling dynamics in other run-reversing bacterial species.
evidence: This is a statement about the applicability of the method.

claim: All work was done with H. pylori PMSS1 strain.
source: All the work was done with H. pylori PMSS1.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental materials.

claim: Cultures of microaerophilic H. pylori were grown in an incubator with controlled temperature and CO2 environment at 10% CO2, 37°C.
source: Cultures of microaerophilic H. pylori were grown in an incubator with controlled temperature and CO2 environment (Benchmark Incu-Shaker Mini CO2). The incubator was maintained at 10% CO2, 37°C.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental methods.

claim: Cells were imaged in a culture-dish on a phase-contrast microscope equipped with a 10X phase objective.
source: Cells were imaged in a culture-dish (Delta T system, Bioptechs Inc) on a phase-contrast microscope (Nikon Optiphot) equipped with a 10X phase objective.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental methods.

claim: Videos were recorded with a CCD camera at 45 frames per second.
source: Videos were recorded with a CCD camera (IDS model UI-3240LE) at 45 frames per second.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental methods.

claim: All experiments were performed at 37°C unless otherwise noted.
source: All experiments were performed at 37°C unless otherwise noted.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental conditions.

claim: The low cell density enabled the use of particle-tracking methods to record the swimming trajectory of each cell.
source: The low cell density enabled us to employ particle-tracking methods to record the swimming trajectory of each cell (Ford et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental approach, supported by a citation.

claim: All videos were analyzed with custom-written MATLAB codes based on centroid-detection-based particle-tracking routines.
source: All the videos were analyzed with custom-written MATLAB codes based on centroid-detection-based particle-tracking routines (Crocker and Grier, 1996).
evidence: This is a statement about the data analysis methods, supported by a citation.
